newsitem.title: UKRAINE: World Bank optimistic on Ukraine foreign borrowing.
newsitem.headline: World Bank optimistic on Ukraine foreign borrowing.

text.p: A top World Bank official said on Tuesday that Ukraine should be able to meet foreign borrowing targets in this year's budget deficit.

"Generally I have a strong view that the deficit...can be financed from sources in the IMF (International Monetary Fund) and the World Bank and in the international debt markets," Paul Siegelbaum, the Bank's new director for Ukraine and Belarus, told his debut news conference in the Ukrainian capital.
But he added that the government would have to meet conditions to do so. "It is within their control," he said.
Ukraine, which has won a poor record with foreign investors scared off by government corruption and ever-changing legislation, failed to pass this year's budget until June 27.

Siegelbaum said it was an important achievement that Ukraine had passed the budget, which set foreign borrowing at 2.4 billion hryvnias ($1.3 billion), revenues at 22.4 billion hryvnias and expenditures at 28.12 billion hryvnias.
But he added that no one involved in the document or who had followed the process of its creation would call it ideal.
The IMF said it might delay a $2.5-$3 billion three-year loan and issue an interim stand-by deal while Ukraine met the rest of a list of 41 of the Fund's conditions.
But the economy ministry said in a statement on Tuesday that Ukraine was continuing talks on the Extended Fund Facility loan with an IMF mission which is due to end on July 10.
Only two of nine tax reform laws have been passed by parliament, on value-added tax and taxation of business profits, and the rest are up for debate by the end of the year.

The Fund wants Ukraine to cut payroll taxes from 52 percent to 40 percent as a first step, in an attempt to legalise the undeclared economy -- estimated by Western analysts to account for up 60 percent of all economic activity.
Asked about Ukraine's chances on the foreign bond market, Siegelbaum said: "Everything can be sold if the price is right."
"The potential investors I have spoken to have all said that they would seriously consider buying bonds issued by Ukraine so long as the interest rate were attractive enough," he added.

Serhiy Tyhypko, deputy prime minister in charge of reforms, told Reuters at an investment conference in Frankfurt earlier on Tuesday that Ukraine would follow up its foreign debt debut in Japan in September with a Eurobond in September or October.

Siegelbaum, fresh from meeting President Leonid Kuchma, said they discussed tremendous problems in the energy sector, in agriculture and in general government efficiency over the budget, tax and decision-making processes.
"We both agreed that even though these problems are very challenging, Ukraine has both the resources and the human capital to address them," he said.
"This is not going to be a quick process and it's going to require many choices that will be cruel," said Siegelbaum.

He urged Ukraine to make sure its legal system was enforced through the courts, but said he would leave Ukraine on Wednesday optimistic that the Bank could continue implementing its projects in the former Soviet republic of 51 million people.
"One of the most encouraging things during my visit was that our discussions were never over whether reforms should occur, but how and when," he said.
World Bank credits to Ukraine total $1.38 billion for seven projects, including coal sector restructuring, agricultural reform, and development of the energy sector. ($ = 1.856 Ukrainian Hryvnias)
